question: After partitioning this array around the highlighted pivot (value 5), which statement is guaranteed true?

options.text: 5 is now at the index it will occupy in the fully sorted array
options.why: Partitioning places the pivot at its final sorted position; that's the invariant quicksort relies on.

options.text: The whole array is now sorted
options.why: Only the pivot's position is finalized — both sides still need to be recursively sorted.

options.text: All elements greater than 5 come before it
options.why: It's the reverse: partitioning puts smaller elements before the pivot and larger ones after.

options.text: The pivot always ends up at index 0
options.why: The pivot's final index depends on how many elements are smaller than it, not a fixed position.

question: A hash table with 1 million keys and a well-distributed hash function has average-case lookup time of:

options.why: A good hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets, so a lookup checks a small constant number of entries.

options.text: O(log n)
options.why: That's the complexity of a balanced search tree, not a hash table.

options.text: O(n)
options.why: That's only the worst case, when most keys collide into the same bucket.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.why: That's a sorting complexity, not a lookup complexity.

question: Why is a linked list a poor choice for binary search compared to an array?

options.text: Binary search needs O(1) random access to jump to the middle element, which a linked list can't provide
options.why: Arrays support constant-time indexing, but a linked list must be walked node-by-node, making the 'jump to the middle' step itself O(n).

options.text: Linked lists can't be sorted
options.why: Linked lists can absolutely be sorted; that's not the issue.

options.text: Binary search only works on numbers, not linked structures
options.why: Binary search works on any comparable, sorted sequence — the data structure isn't the constraint.

options.text: Linked lists use more memory per element
options.why: True in general, but irrelevant to why binary search specifically fails here — the issue is access pattern, not memory.

question: What does `git rebase` do that `git merge` does not?

options.text: Rewrites commit history to create a linear sequence instead of a merge commit
options.why: Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a linear history; merge instead adds a new commit joining both histories.

options.text: Deletes the original branch
options.why: Neither command deletes a branch by default.

options.text: Pushes your changes to the remote automatically
options.why: Both are local operations; neither pushes on its own.

options.text: Only works on the main branch
options.why: Rebase works on any branch, not just main.

question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from n unsorted elements (heapify)?

options.text: O(n)
options.why: Although each sift-down looks like O(log n), most nodes are near the bottom of the tree and need little work, so the total sums to a linear bound.

options.text: O(n log n)
options.why: That's the naive per-element upper bound before accounting for most nodes being near the leaves.

options.text: O(log n)
options.why: That's the cost of a single insert or extract, not building the whole heap.
That would only be true for a badly implemented sift-up-from-scratch approach, not standard heapify.

question: A B-tree index is most useful for which kind of query?

options.text: Range queries like `WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30`
options.why: A B-tree keeps keys in sorted order, so a range scan can walk consecutive leaf entries directly.

options.text: Exact-match lookups only, never ranges
options.why: B-trees handle both; a hash index is the one limited to exact matches.

options.text: Full-text search across large text columns
options.why: That's the job of a specialized text/inverted index, not a general B-tree.

options.text: Queries with no WHERE clause at all
options.why: An index isn't used at all when there's no filtering condition to apply it to.

question: What does the CAP theorem say a distributed system must give up during a network partition?

options.text: Either consistency or availability, but not both
options.why: CAP states that under a partition you can guarantee at most one of consistency and availability, alongside partition tolerance which isn't optional.

options.text: Partition tolerance
options.why: Partition tolerance isn't optional in a real distributed system — the tradeoff is between the other two.

options.text: Durability
options.why: Durability isn't one of the three properties CAP is about (Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance).

options.text: Nothing — a well-designed system keeps all three
options.why: That's exactly what CAP proves is impossible during an actual partition.

question: Why does appending to a Python list have amortized O(1) time even though the underlying array sometimes needs to be resized?

options.text: When resizing happens, the list grows by a multiple of its current size, so the cost of occasional resizes is spread thinly across many cheap appends
options.why: Geometric growth means resize frequency drops as the list grows, and the total copying cost stays proportional to n over n appends.

options.text: Python lists never actually resize; they pre-allocate infinite space
options.why: Lists do resize — Python just pads extra capacity so it isn't on every single append.

options.text: Because append always inserts at the front, which is naturally fast
options.why: append adds to the end; inserting at the front is the O(n) operation, not append.

options.text: Because the list is implemented as a linked list under the hood
options.why: CPython lists are backed by a contiguous array, not a linked list.

question: What problem does two-phase commit (2PC) solve in distributed databases?

options.text: Getting all participating nodes to agree on committing or aborting the same transaction
options.why: 2PC's prepare/commit phases ensure every participant either all commits or all aborts, avoiding a state where nodes disagree.

options.text: Load balancing requests across replicas
options.why: That's a routing/load-balancing concern, unrelated to transaction agreement.

options.text: Encrypting data in transit between nodes
options.why: 2PC is a coordination protocol, not a security mechanism.

options.text: Automatically sharding a table across nodes
options.why: Sharding is a data-distribution strategy, separate from commit coordination.

question: In this array, what does the two-pointer technique conclude about whether it's a palindrome?

options.text: It is a palindrome — pointers meet in the middle with all matching pairs
options.why: Comparing values at the left and right pointers (1&1, 2&2) as they move inward finds every pair equal, confirming a palindrome.

options.text: It is not a palindrome
options.why: Every mirrored pair (index 0&4, 1&3) matches, so it is a palindrome.

options.text: The technique doesn't apply to arrays with an odd length

options.text: It would require O(n^2) time to check
options.why: Two pointers check a palindrome in O(n) time, one pass inward from both ends.

question: Why can two dictionaries with the same keys and values still fail an `is` comparison but pass `==`?

options.text: `==` compares their contents, while `is` checks whether they're the same object in memory — two separately created dicts are equal in value but different objects
options.why: Value equality and identity are different checks; equal content doesn't imply the same memory address.

options.text: Dictionaries can never be compared with `==`
options.why: Dictionaries support `==` just fine, comparing keys and values.

options.text: `is` and `==` behave identically for dictionaries
options.why: They diverge specifically when two distinct objects happen to hold equal values.

options.text: It's a bug in Python that will be fixed
options.why: This is intended, well-documented behavior, not a bug.

question: What does a covering index let a database avoid doing?

options.text: Going back to the main table to fetch additional columns, since the index itself contains everything the query needs
options.why: If every column the query selects and filters on is already in the index, the engine can answer entirely from the index without a lookup into the table's heap.

options.text: Using any WHERE clause at all
options.why: Covering indexes still support filtering; the benefit is about avoiding an extra table lookup, not filtering.

options.text: Writing to the table
options.why: A covering index affects read performance, not write behavior directly.

options.text: Sorting the result set
options.why: Sorting is a separate concern from whether a lookup needs to touch the base table.

question: Why do database transactions use the 'Isolation' property of ACID?

options.text: So that concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted intermediate changes
options.why: Isolation ensures each transaction behaves as if it ran alone, preventing issues like dirty reads from other in-flight transactions.

options.text: So that a crash doesn't lose committed data
options.why: That's the Durability property, not Isolation.

options.text: So that a transaction either fully completes or fully rolls back
options.why: That's Atomicity.

options.text: So that the database enforces valid data constraints
options.why: That's closer to Consistency, not Isolation.

question: What is the main advantage of a trie over a hash set for storing a dictionary of words?

options.text: It supports efficient prefix queries, like finding all words starting with 'pre'
options.why: A trie's structure directly mirrors shared prefixes, so walking down from the root naturally enumerates or checks prefixes; a hash set has no such structure.

options.text: It uses less memory than a hash set in every case
options.why: Tries often use more memory than a hash set due to per-character node overhead.

options.text: It has faster average-case single-word lookup than a hash set
options.why: A hash set's O(1) average lookup is at least as fast; the trie's edge is prefix operations, not raw lookup speed.

options.text: It keeps words in insertion order
options.why: Neither structure is defined by preserving insertion order; that's not the reason to pick a trie.

question: Does missing the review on one card delay a related card's FSRS due date?

options.text: No — each card's schedule is independent; a miss on one card never delays another card's due date
options.why: FSRS state is tracked per card; a sibling miss is surfaced as a 'drill this topic' suggestion instead of touching another card's schedule.

options.text: Yes — missing one card automatically pushes back every related card's next review
options.why: That would let one bad review distort spacing for other cards, which spaced-repetition systems specifically avoid.

options.text: Only if the cards share the exact same topic tag
options.why: Schedule independence isn't conditional on shared topics — it's true for every card regardless of grouping.

options.text: It depends on which review mode was used
options.why: Review mode changes how a question is asked, not whether FSRS schedules stay independent across cards.
